outline.description: Introduces the radio-interference problem the patents address, summarizes the asserted patents and their key claim requirements, and identifies the accused Nokia PIM-C functionality and the technical signals/components central to the dispute.
subtopics: Intermodulation products (IMPs) and passive intermodulation (PIM): what they are and typical physical causes
’134 patent overview: isolating signals of interest and interference-generating signals; estimating and canceling inband IMPs; closed-loop phase/amplitude adjustment with sub-sample phase shifts

’775 patent overview: co-located transmitter/receiver; generating IMP cancellation signals continuously and near real time from copies of transmitter signals; n-th order ICS via seven specified third-order multiplications of three signals S1, S2, S3
Accused functionality: Nokia PIM-C feature in AT&T’s deployed radios
Key signals/components in Nokia materials: DL(TX) reference, modeled PIM path, x1 and x2, RF ADC, complex conjugate (′) and modulus (|·|)
Location of PIM model generation (GROOT FPGA) versus the RF ADC sampling point

outline.chapter_title: Procedural Posture and Standards of Review
outline.description: Traces the case through trial and post-trial motions to appeal, and sets out the governing standards the Federal Circuit applied to evaluate JMOL, infringement findings, claim construction, and damages.
subtopics: Claims asserted: ’134 patent claims 1–3; ’775 patent claims 1, 4, 9, 16, 21, 29, 36
Jury verdict: validity and infringement on all asserted claims; lump-sum damages of $166,303,391
Post-trial motions: JMOL of noninfringement and damages; motion for new trial on damages; district court denies all
Appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1)
JMOL standard (Fifth Circuit law): de novo review; reversal only if evidence overwhelmingly favors one side; substantial-evidence review for jury infringement findings
Claim construction: de novo, with clear-error review for underlying factual findings
Damages review: new-trial denial reviewed for abuse of discretion; effect of noninfringement on damages

outline.chapter_title: Infringement Analysis—’134 Patent: Failure to Prove Sampling of Both Required Signal Categories
outline.description: Explains why the Federal Circuit found insufficient evidence that the accused radios met claim 1[a] of the ’134 patent, focusing on the expert’s inconsistent mapping of the claimed signal categories to the accused system and the temporal impossibility flagged on cross-examination.
subtopics: Claim 1[a] requirement: receiver must oversample a passband that includes both signals of interest and interference-generating signals
Finesse’s mapping at trial: signals of interest = DL(TX) reference; interference-generating signals = modeled PIM path; both allegedly enter the RF ADC
Temporal/architectural flaw: modeled PIM path is generated downstream (in the FPGA) after ADC sampling; cannot be sampled before it exists

Cross-examination pivot: expert references x1 and x2 as two inputs but does not clearly map them to the claim-recited categories; continues to identify modeled PIM path as the interference-generating signals
District court’s JMOL ruling: infers expert meant x1/x2 as the two claim-recited signal categories; finds sufficient evidence

Federal Circuit reasoning: testimony remained confusing and self-contradictory; no clear, consistent mapping to both required categories; Johns Hopkins v. Datascope principle that self-contradictory expert testimony cannot sustain a verdict
Disposition on ’134 patent: reversal of denial of JMOL—no substantial evidence of infringement

outline.chapter_title: Infringement Analysis—’775 Patent: ‘Three Signals’ and the Seven Required Multiplications
outline.description: Details the dispute over the ‘three signals’ and the seven specified multiplications in claim 1[d] of the ’775 patent, the district court’s claim construction, the prosecution-history argument, and why the Federal Circuit concluded the proof did not show all seven multiplications.
subtopics: Claim 1[d] requirement: generate an n-th order ICS via seven third-order multiplications of three signals S1, S2, S3
Claim construction: ‘S1, S2 and S3’ must be separately identifiable, not necessarily unique; district court’s waiver finding on a ‘uniqueness’ argument
Prosecution history/disavowal: amendment from ‘two or three’ to ‘three’ signals; Federal Circuit finds no clear and unambiguous surrender of non-unique inputs (Continental Circuits standard)
Finesse’s proof: Nokia document shows only three distinct multiplications (x1·|x1|·|x1|; x1·x1·x2′; x1·|x2|·|x2|) involving modulus and complex conjugates

Mapping gap: no trial testimony connecting those three operations to the seven specifically listed products; appellate mapping attempts are not trial evidence and require impermissible substitutions (e.g., equating x2, x2′, and |x2| with the same S-signal)
‘Ten multiplications’ argument (coefficients a0–a9): no identification of which subset corresponds to the seven claimed products or how they map to the three distinct operations actually shown
Disposition on ’775 patent: reversal of denial of JMOL—insufficient evidence that all seven claimed multiplications are performed

outline.description: Addresses the remedy flowing from the noninfringement rulings and distills practice-oriented lessons about expert proof and claim mapping in complex signal-processing patent cases.
subtopics: Consequences for damages: vacatur of the $166,303,391 lump-sum award
Final disposition: reversed (noninfringement) and vacated (damages); costs to Appellants
Expert testimony lessons: maintain clear, consistent mappings from accused system elements to each claim limitation; avoid contradictions and post hoc clarifications on appeal
Technical proof in DSP contexts: establish when and where signals exist relative to claimed operations; prove every enumerated operation (e.g., all seven multiplications), not just a subset
Claim drafting and litigation strategy: amendments adding specificity do not necessarily disavow broader scope absent clear statements; preserve arguments to avoid waiver disputes
